title: Curves: Map, Clock, Frame
notes: Open by separating three layers that students often merge: the moving point alpha, the clock t that drives it, and the geometric data that survive after a regular change of clock. The chapter source span is broad, so the lecture should feel like a route map rather than a list of formulas.

title: The Trace Does Not Remember The Clock
notes: Use the three traces to make the first diagnostic concrete. A circle run twice has the same image as a circle run once but a different velocity signal. A cusp can look like an ordinary drawing until the speed test exposes the stalled tangent at the singular point.

title: Regularity Certifies Tangent Geometry
notes: Stress that regularity is not a decorative hypothesis. It is the certificate that the tangent line is actually defined at the parameter value under discussion. Once alpha prime is nonzero, the velocity vector gives both a direction on the trace and a denominator for arclength differentiation.

title: Arclength Turns Motion Into A Ruler
notes: Present arclength as a cumulative measuring device attached to the curve. The graph of s against t is the useful object: strict increase comes from positive speed, and that strict increase is exactly what lets the old clock be replaced by distance traveled.

title: Reparametrization Changes Speed, Not Length
notes: Connect the chain rule to the geometric invariant. A valid clock change rescales velocity by phi prime, so instantaneous speed changes, but the accumulated length does not. This slide prepares the habit of checking which quantities are clock signals and which are geometric signals.

title: Unit Speed Makes The First Formula Quiet
notes: Once the curve is reparametrized by arclength, the tangent vector has norm one. Differentiate that identity to show why the change in tangent is perpendicular to the tangent itself. This is the clean doorway into normal direction and curvature.

title: Frenet Data Packages Local Motion
notes: Build the frame in the order a computation would use: tangent from velocity, normal from the derivative of tangent, and binormal from the oriented cross product. The point is not memorizing a triad; it is seeing how local motion becomes an orthonormal coordinate system carried by the curve.

title: Curvature And Torsion Are Calibration Signals
notes: Use the helix as the calibration object. Its curvature and torsion are constant, so it gives an immediate sanity check for formulas and numerical samples. Curvature measures tangent turning per unit length, while torsion measures rotation of the osculating plane through the binormal.

title: Local Canonical Form Is A Microscope
notes: Frame coordinates turn Taylor expansion into geometry. The s term records tangent displacement, the s squared term records curvature toward the normal, and the s cubed term begins to reveal torsion through binormal displacement. This is local shape information, not a new parametrization trick.

title: The Osculating Circle Reads Kappa
notes: Explain the osculating circle as the circle with second order contact at the chosen point. It shares position, tangent, and curvature direction. A large radius means small bending, and an infinite limiting radius is the geometric picture behind zero curvature.

title: Plane Curves Carry A Turning Ledger
notes: For plane curves, the unit tangent can be encoded by a tangent angle theta. Integrating the signed rate of change gives a global turning count. The local curvature signal therefore becomes a ledger for how the whole closed curve winds its tangent direction.

title: Global Tests Catch More Than Local Smoothness
notes: Move from local definitions to diagnostics that inspect an entire trace. Rotation index, total curvature, convexity, and vertex counts ask whether local bending data is organized globally. The notebook examples are chosen to make these tests visible without relying on copied exercises.

title: Bad Clocks And Singular Samples
notes: Return to the warning that the same plotted image can hide different parameter behavior. A clock that stops creates zero speed even when the trace looks familiar. The numerical habit is to inspect speed before trusting tangent, curvature, or any derivative divided by speed.

title: Inspect The 3D Frame, Not Just The Trace
notes: The helix frame is useful because torsion is difficult to see in a fixed two dimensional projection. Ask students to rotate the interactive artifact and track how T, N, and B move together. The visual target is the twisting osculating plane, not the helix shape alone.

title: A Short Board Audit
notes: Use this slide as a compact in-class audit rather than a long exercise. Students should identify which claims depend only on the trace and which depend on the clock. The goal is to make regularity, arclength, curvature, and total turning feel like a checklist for a new curve.

title: Recap: Local Data, Global Tests
notes: Close by walking through the dependency chain one last time. Start with a parametrized map, certify regularity, replace the clock by arclength when useful, build Frenet data, read local shape through curvature and torsion, and finally integrate or compare those signals to make global conclusions.
